nameStory: The Familiar Bluet earned its common name because it's one of the most commonly encountered and easily recognized members of the bluet group of damselflies. The word 'bluet' comes from the distinctive bright blue coloration that males display, while 'familiar' reflects how frequently people spot this species around ponds and lakes throughout its range.
description: The Familiar Bluet is a slender damselfly with delicate, narrow wings that fold back along its body when at rest. Males are bright blue with black markings, while females can be blue, green, or brownish with similar dark patterns. These dainty insects are about 1-1.5 inches long with thread-like bodies and large, prominent eyes. Unlike their dragonfly cousins, bluets have a weak, fluttering flight pattern and prefer to perch on vegetation near water.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Wings fold back along the body when perched, rather than held out perpendicular like dragonflies. The wings feel papery-thin and are completely clear with delicate black veining.

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Bright sky-blue body with bold black stripes and spots. The blue has an almost metallic sheen in sunlight, contrasting sharply with jet-black markings on the thorax and segments.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely slender, stick-like abdomen that feels surprisingly delicate if handled gently. The body is much thinner than a pencil and segments are clearly visible.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, bulging compound eyes that are widely separated (unlike dragonflies whose eyes touch). Eyes appear glossy black or dark blue and take up much of the head.

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttery flight that looks almost moth-like. They rarely fly far from water and tend to flutter from plant to plant rather than soaring.

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often perches vertically on thin stems or grass blades near water's edge. Will land on your finger if you move slowly and remain still.

habitat: Look for Familiar Bluets around still or slow-moving freshwater including ponds, lakes, marshes, and quiet stream backwaters throughout New England. They prefer areas with abundant emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and water lilies where they can easily perch and hunt for small flying insects. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations, especially in areas with some sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May and early June as waters warm. Look for recently emerged individuals with their wings still soft and bodies not yet fully colored.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are mating, laying eggs, and most visible. This is the best time to observe their courtship behaviors and see the striking color differences between males and females.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into September and early October, though numbers decline. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with faded colors and tattered wing edges.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with first hard frosts. Nymphs (juveniles) spend winter underwater in mud and debris, developing slowly until ready to emerge the following spring.

funFact: Male Familiar Bluets perform an elaborate courtship dance where they hover in front of females while rapidly vibrating their wings to create a buzzing sound - essentially serenading potential mates with their wing music, much like crickets do with their legs!
confusionNotes: Familiar Bluets are easily confused with other blue damselflies in the Enallagma genus, but they're generally the most common and widespread species you'll encounter. Memory trick: if you see a blue damselfly near water in New England, your first guess should be Familiar Bluet since they live up to their name. The key is looking at specific marking patterns rather than just the blue color.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bluets,' not all individuals are blue - females often appear green, brown, or tan, which can confuse beginners who expect all bluets to be blue. This color variation in females is actually an evolutionary strategy to avoid harassment from overeager males of their own and other species.
compareHints: Familiar Bluets are distinguished from other Enallagma species primarily by their black stripe patterns on the thorax and the shape of blue markings on their abdominal segments. They're generally more robust than Little Bluets and lack the distinctive orange coloration of Orange Bluets. The male's bright blue color and widespread habitat preferences make them the 'default' bluet species in most New England locations.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many bluet species, Azure Bluets stand out for their particularly vibrant blue coloration with relatively simple black banding patterns.
Among New England's many bluet species, Skimming Bluets are best distinguished by behavior rather than appearance alone.
Among New England's many bluet species, Stream Bluets are distinguished by their habitat preference for moving water and the blue abdominal tips on both sexes.
Among New England bluets, Orange Bluet males are unmistakable due to their orange coloration, while species like Familiar Bluet and Azure Bluet remain blue with black markings.
Among New England's many bluets, marsh bluets are distinguished by their specific habitat preferences and the particular pattern of black markings on males.
Among New England's many bluet species, Vesper Bluets are distinguished by their specific abdominal markings and habitat preferences for still waters.

Among New England's many bluet species, the New England Bluet is distinguished by its specific shoulder stripe pattern and habitat preferences, though reliable identification often requires examining microscopic details.
Among New England's many bluet species, Hagen's bluet can be distinguished by its specific abdominal marking pattern, though this requires close examination or good photographs.
Among the many New England bluets, the Slender Bluet stands out for its particularly fine, thread-like build that makes other bluets look chunky by comparison.
Among the 24 bluet species potentially found in New England, scarlet bluet is the only one with prominent red markings, making identification relatively straightforward.
Among the many New England bluets, Little Bluet stands out primarily for its diminutive size - it's consistently smaller than familiar species like Azure Bluets or Familiar Bluets.
Among the many bluets in New England, the turquoise bluet is distinguished by its greenish-blue coloration rather than the pure blues of species like the familiar bluet or azure bluet.
Among the many bluet species, Tule Bluets are distinguished by their strong association with emergent marsh vegetation and their specific thoracic markings.

Atlantic Bluets are distinguished from other Enallagma bluets by their specific black markings pattern - they typically have more extensive black on the thorax shoulders compared to Familiar Bluets, and less black on the abdomen tip than Azure Bluets.
